Senses.Explanation: The matter has no single fixed direction marks a turn away from treating one response or stance as universally binding. Fayan and Yuanwu use the phrase after an uncompromising statement to reopen responsive action. Across four independent sayings records, the phrase licenses a context-sensitive turn without denying the matter itself.

Senses.Explanation: The disciplinary code is the body of monastic rules by which conduct is measured. Xuzhou Xingsheng defines carrying out what has been disclosed so that conduct does not go astray as ‘code’ (律). Guxue Zhenzhe cites its requirement that one who has received precepts remain under the conferring authorities, and Fayan Wenyi turns its rule about hearing ornaments through a wall into a public question about violation. Zhongfeng Mingben says Baizhang's monastic regulations drew on this code to establish ritual forms. The records also bend the category: Wuxie Lingmo answers whether he resides according to Chan or the code by saying that he neither keeps the code nor sits dhyana, while Dazhu Huihai warns that a code master can bind himself by keeping it. The rule remains concrete even when masters test what keeping it does.

Senses.Explanation: Disciplinary rules are the hard forms that regulate conduct; Chan records preserve them as rules that can be received, followed, broken, or falsely dismissed in the name of freedom. Zhongfeng Mingben criticizes people who break the disciplinary rules and violate prohibitions without fear, then later rejects the opposite error of making secondary observance into a fixed mechanism. His two warnings keep the rule hard without making it the whole Chan test. Zhuanyu Guanheng explicitly glosses the title Daily Disciplinary Rules as the ordinary forms for maintaining conduct in daily use so it is not lost. In a raised case, Shakyamuni Buddha says two monastics have violated the disciplinary rules; Poshan Haiming then reworks how their expulsion and the subsequent request for teaching would be handled. Biographies also record receiving, following, or refusing such rules as concrete acts rather than abstract category.

A Vinaya master is a specialist in monastic discipline who may serve as an ordination teacher or preceptor. The records say that Nanyue Huairang entered monastic life under Vinaya master Hongjing, that Huineng received ordination from Vinaya master Zhiguang, and that Zhantang went to Vinaya master Kang'an for full ordination. The Jingde Lamp Record also places Vinaya master Guangtong in an adversarial exchange with Bodhidharma, while Dazhu Huihai's record has Vinaya master Faming challenge Dazhu Huihai. Those exchanges make particular Vinaya masters opponents; they do not make every Vinaya master a foil by definition.
Senses.Note: Ordination teacher, discipline specialist, and interlocutor all concern the same institutional role. The hostile Bodhidharma narrative is one inherited deployment repeated across lamp recensions and counts once.

Senses.Explanation: 王法 is the ruler’s law or the public law of the realm. Xuansha Shibei answers a monk by calling him ‘a criminal under royal law.’ Guxue Zhenzhe distinguishes two kinds of law, 王法 and 佛法, while an administrator in the Fengxue case says that Buddha-law and royal law are alike. Lingyan Chonggui’s ‘royal law has no favorites’ and Huotang Yan’s refusal that it recognizes old and young both stress its impartial force.

A familiar personal designation for Nanquan Puyuan, whose lay surname was Wang. Nanquan uses the designation of himself in the third person, while Xuefeng Huikong, Yuanwu Keqin, Xisou Shaotan, Zhongfeng Mingben, Yulin Tongxiu, and Miyun Yuanwu quote or redeploy it as Nanquan's familiar name.
Senses.Note: It does not identify an otherwise unknown teacher surnamed Wang; the surrounding buffalo, spirit, self-sale, and examination stories belong to their individual passages.

Senses.Explanation: To see one's own nature. Chan records place this claim in transmission formulas, instructions, questions, and explicit challenges. Hongren links it with directly becoming a buddha; a text attributed to Bodhidharma says that seeking a buddha requires it. Huangbo Xiyun answers a direct question by refusing to make nature a second object seen by a separate seeing subject. Dahui Zonggao repeats that it is required for an unerring road and immediately asks which mind recognizes and which nature is seen. Zhongfeng Mingben says direct pointing is no longer direct once it enters speech or contrivance, while Yongming Yanshou says that once nature is seen, mind and the teaching remedies both cease. The phrase names a claimed recognition, but the records repeatedly test what the grammar of a seer looking at a separate nature would wrongly add.

Senses.Explanation: The four ordinary functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, named together as a fixed sequence. Wuxiang warns that interpreting the matter in terms of these functions is far from the Way, yet his verse says the same functions are unobstructed. Langye Huijue calls them both causes of birth and death and the basis of liberation, while Dazhu Huihai says a person is not bound by them. Zhongfeng Mingben identifies mind itself with seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing and says not to posit another so-called seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing above them. Huineng says the six faculties perform these functions without being stained by the many objects. In a clearly marked quotation, Dahui Zonggao cites Vimalakirti’s statement that the teaching cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known. These opposed predicates show that the sequence itself is neutral: it names the four functions, not bondage or liberation.

Senses.Explanation: Seeing the tracks is the second oxherding stage: the seeker has found signs of the ox but has not yet caught it. Oxherding sequences place it after seeking the ox and before seeing or catching the ox. Their headings, prefaces, and verses describe tracks beside water or in wild country as an initial but incomplete disclosure. The stage explanations explicitly call it provisional and distinguish seeing traces from direct possession. The corpus's own sequence fixes the stage's observable job.

Senses.Note: Two exact works use seeing traces outside the oxherding-stage title, once for traces appearing with mental turning and once for traces that remain after knowing where to return.

Senses.Explanation: To see the Way is to reach or manifest the recognition that the retained records call seeing, rather than ordinary eyesight. Bodhidharma's attributed teaching calls seeing no thing “seeing the Way”; Yang Jie's preface calls one who understands the single true mind a person who sees the Way; another exchange says attachment to appearances prevents it. Sikong Benjing and Dahui Zonggao pair seeing the Way with cultivating it, Nanyue Huairang rejects seeing it through formation and decay, Shending Hongyin says subtle understanding is not yet seeing it, and Yuan'an Liao uses the phrase in a verse on the dragon's roar in a dry tree.

Senses.Explanation: To disclose or show something, including instruction shown in a public interview. An unnamed monk asks Baizhang Yuansu to disclose the intention of the patriarch’s coming from the west and receives “the mud ox swallows the huge wave”; the named layman He Changbai asks Juelang Daosheng for instruction for the Fushan assembly and receives a verse about clouds and snow. In the Longtan–Tianhuang case, Longtan Chongxin complains that he has long attended without being shown the essentials of mind. Tianhuang Daowu lists raising a hand when tea was brought and lowering his head when greeted, then asks, “Where was I not showing you the essentials of mind?” (那裏不是與你開示心要處). The Blue Cliff Record's compiler narrates that Jingqing Daofu used a responsive dynamic to “show later students” (開示後學); Jingqing is the person described, not the utterer of that clause. The monastery manager Chengyi tells Jifei Ruyi that he has received Jifei’s disclosure (承師開示), treating Jifei’s reply as instruction already given. Request, act, repeated conduct, and received instruction are stages of the same showing, not different lexical referents.

Permission and prohibition name the paired work of allowing and barring under a rule. Yulin Tongxiu says that rigid attachment obscures the purpose of permission and prohibition and prevents recognition of what the Buddha established. Shishuang Chuyuan uses the pair for Linji's four selections, which open or bar according to the hearer's capacity. Zhongfeng Mingben refuses an appeal to permission, prohibition, keeping, and violation that would make them excuses for lawlessness. Yongming Yanshou also uses the pair for distinctions made within the teaching while saying that first-principle emptiness itself leaves no tracks. The pair thus serves both the precept rule and Chan's controlled opening and barring.
Senses.Note: The precept and Chan cases retain one paired operation—allowing and barring—applied in distinct settings; context alone does not prove two different things.
